We looked for comprehensive data sets covering a range of conditions in order to eliminate biases in the results. In an atmospheric dispersion scenario, data can be categorized as either known parameters describing the released material at the source or measurements of a dispersing cloud taken downwind such as contaminant concentration or cloud dimensions. Data was available from both controlled field experiments and real-world accidents. Either type of data set may not be reliable in measuring model performance when simulating differing conditions. To limit this effect, a variety of conditions were sought based on the following criteria: • Measurements taken at numerous and varied downwind distances • A variety of source conditions such as release amounts, time durations, and chemical material • A range of atmospheric conditions, namely stability and wind speed 13 LLNL-TR-818768 The final validation data came from two field studies, Desert Tortoise (field tests 1, 2, and 4) and Goldfish (field tests 1, 2, and 3), and a set of real-world rail car accidents (Hanna, 2008). All three data sets provided comprehensive source information as well as results from other dense gas models for comparison. The field studies also provided downwind measurements, a standard for comparison with results from the new capability. All the field study and real world case scenarios also took place in similar surroundings, relatively flat, rural, open areas. EPIcode’s default parameterization (“Standard” terrain) for turbulence conveniently describes these conditions and as a result remained as such throughout all the validation calculations. Modeling results provided here would therefore not be appropriate for urban environments or other terrains. 3.2 Comparison of EPIcode Results to the Validation Data 3.2.1 Desert Tortoise In 1983, a major series of field experiments involving atmospheric releases of ammonia, Desert Tortoise, was performed in the Nevada desert by the U.S. Department of Energy at the Liquefied Gaseous Fuels Test Facility (Goldwire, et al., 1983; Zapert, et al., 1991). Table 3.1 shows the release parameters for the three Desert Tortoise experiments (experiments 1, 2, and 4) used as input into EPIcode for the comparison calculations. Each experiment used large quantities of liquid ammonia (greater than 3,000 gallons), necessary to trigger a dense gas release, but with variations in amount released, time duration of the release, wind speed, and sample time (the time period over which plume concentration is estimated or measured).
